Hi Alyssa —

Thanks again for taking the call yesterday. To get Marissa (our pre-sales SE) and Dev (runtime lead) what they need for a dedicated fleet projection, could you share a short traffic snapshot? A CSV with the following would be ideal: hourly request counts for a typical weekday and weekend, 95th percentile response length (tokens), and any daily burst events (time windows + multiplier).

If it's easier, the three fields we most care about are:
- Peak concurrent sessions (peak 5-minute window)
- Average prompt length and average response length (tokens)
- Latency SLO target at P95 (ms)

Attached is a quick checklist (redwood-mvp-sizing-checklist.pdf) that explains how we use each item. If you can drop the CSV into the Drive link or reply inline, we can run a ballpark projection quickly.

Goal: provide a preliminary GPU pool recommendation and an estimated monthly commit within 48 hours.

Hi Michael —

Thanks — attaching a small sample CSV (finova-mrp-traffic-snapshot.csv) and past-week summary. Quick answers in case Marissa/Dev want to see them without opening the file:
- Peak concurrent sessions: ~220 (observed 5-min peak at 11:15am PST last Wednesday).
- Prompt length: avg 45 tokens (mostly short search-style prompts)
- Response length: avg 320 tokens, 95th pct ~980 tokens
- SLA target: P95 latency <= 800ms (the product team wants sub-second in interactive flows; batch/async can be relaxed)

We also have two scheduled batch windows overnight for bulk scoring (~midnight and 03:00) that spike total QPS but not concurrency. Let us know if you need more columns from our telemetry.

Hi Alyssa — thanks for the CSV, that helps a lot. A couple of follow-ups so we don't over- or under-provision: 

1) Can you confirm how many of the concurrent sessions are interactive vs async (approx %)? Interactive sessions require low latency and cannot tolerate batching that adds 200–400ms.
2) For the 95th token length (~980 tokens) — is that from a single long-response workflow (one request -> long output) or concatenated multi-request flows?
3) Do you use streaming for responses today? Streaming changes how we budget NVMe and network egress for long-lived streams.

Dev, FYI: if they have 220 peak concurrent interactive sessions and a P95 target of 800ms on ~320 tok responses, rough back-of-envelope suggests we should consider a mix of A100-equivalent machines with 16–32 GPUs and aggressive KV caching. I'll run two scenarios: conservative (10% headroom) and aggressive (30% headroom).

Alyssa — if you can just reply inline to the three questions above that will let us produce a preliminary fleet map and an estimated monthly commit.

Thanks,
Marissa
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

From: Tom Reyes <tom.reyes@finova-analytics.com>

Subject: Re: Dedicated GPU sizing: initial probe for peak concurrency and latency targets

Marissa — quick answers from our infra lead: 

1) Interactive vs async: ~65% interactive, 35% async/queue workers.
2) 95th token length: mostly single long response requests (user asks for long summaries occasionally); we do not concatenate multiple requests into one response.
3) We currently stream responses to the client for long outputs (important for UX).

Also FYI: peak concurrency tends to be regional — California offices + small EU office. If you model US peak first that's fine. We've redacted some PII in the CSV.

We'll need an estimate of the expected monthly commit and a short mutual action plan that lists deliverables and timing so procurement can review.

- Tom
Tom Reyes
VP Engineering | Finova Analytics
